It even wrote "text likely spans only the first 200-300 pixels from the left, which means it probably doesn't extend far enough into the darker gradient regions where contrast would become a real problem," yet flipped to "the tail of the text falls over backdrop values in the (96-116,96-116,255) range" and returned REPRODUCED on an admitted guess ("I'm estimating the text boundaries from relatively small crops"). classified.rule: e88epe — Image not in the accessibility tree is decorative

classified.rule: 5effbb  Link in context is descriptive

The model reasoned over this misleading context and never saw the word that resolves the link's purpose.

classified.rule: 5effbb  Link in context is descriptive
classified.realBarrier:
ACT 5effbb tests whether a link's purpose is determinable from its accessible name PLUS its programmatically-determinable context. The link `Workshop` sits alone in its own `

classified.harnessAction: LLM returned NOT REPRODUCED / LIKELY_OK conf=high: "The link 'Workshop' has a specific, descriptive accessible name that, together with its surrounding sentence context ('The W3C held a Workshop'), clearly conveys its destination and purpose."
classified.mechanism: The model applied a generic-name test, not the in-context-descriptiveness test: THINK says "The accessible name 'Workshop' is not generic... it's a specific descriptor" and "This seems specific enough to not be a generic link name failure." It pulled context from a SEPARATE paragraph ("The W3C held a Workshop") which is not the link's programmatic context, and never noticed the href targets `workshop-report.html`, so it cleared a destination the name does not convey.
classified.recommendation: Tighten the link-purpose-v0 rubric so "name is not a generic phrase" is NOT sufficient: require that the destination be conveyed by the accessible name plus the link's OWN programmatic context (enclosing paragraph/sentence), surface the href so the model can detect name-vs-destination mismatch (e.g. "Workshop" vs workshop-report), and forbid borrowing context from sibling paragraphs.

that precedes the

classified.rule: 36b590  Error message describes invalid form field value

Yet under error-identification-v0 that correct ambiguity reasoning only yielded UNCERTAIN/PARTIAL for the Billing subjects and outright LIKELY_OK high for the Shipping subjects ("clearly identified in text", line 42), so the same ambiguous static message never converted into a flagged barrier.
classified.recommendation: Amend the error-identification-v0 rubric so that an error message naming only a field TYPE shared by multiple fields (cannot disambiguate which instance is invalid) and/or an unconditionally-present static error span is scored REPRODUCED (barrier) rather than LIKELY_OK/UNCERTAIN.

classified.rule: fd3a94
classified.realBarrier: fd3a94 fails only when same-named, same-context links do NOT serve EQUIVALENT PURPOSE — different URL is necessary but not sufficient. Here the two "ACT rules" links go to act-rules.github.io and www.w3.org/community/act-r/ — both about the ACT Rules project, so they serve equivalent purpose; W3C raw.json scores this testcase expected:"passed". There is no barrier: equivalent purpose is a semantic judgment that byte-inequality of URL/origin cannot settle.

It treated different origin/finalUrlEqual=false as conclusive.

The THINK line "These are clearly different destinations... go to different websites. This is the classic identical-names-different-destination failure mode" maps different-destination straight to barrier — exactly what link-purpose-v0.md line 26 instructs ("two 'ACT rules' links to different sites" as a FAIL example), conflating "DIFFERENT destinations / serve DIFFERENT purposes" while the rule turns on equivalent purpose.
classified.recommendation: Rewrite link-purpose-v0.md's identical-names mode so different-destination is necessary-but-not-sufficient: require an explicit equivalent-purpose judgment (same topic/equivalent resource across different URLs = NOT a barrier), and remove/invert the "two 'ACT rules' links to different sites" example since that exact fd3a94 fixture is GT-passed.

classified.rule: fd3a94
classified.realBarrier: ACT fd3a94 tests SC 2.4.4 link purpose for two+ same-context links sharing an identical accessible name: it FAILS when those links do not serve equivalent purpose. In this fixture both "contact us" links share one href (distinctRawHrefs=1) but the prose context explicitly promises two different purposes — "contact us via chat" vs "contact us by phone" — while both resolve to the same generic contact-us.html. GT=failed: the identical names in a context that implies distinct chat/phone destinations are ambiguous/misleading, so the real barrier is the name+context mismatch, NOT the href equality.
classified.harnessAction: The LLM returned NOT REPRODUCED (LIKELY_OK, medium) under rubric link-purpose-v0, concluding "Both 'contact us' links share the same raw href (distinctRawHrefs = 1)... so identical names do not create a barrier."
classified.mechanism: The rubric's decision rule is the source of the miss: the model cites "the rubric's rule that identical names to the SAME destination is not a failure" and concludes NOT REPRODUCED. It applied same-href⇒same-purpose⇒pass literally and never weighed the in-fixture context cues ("via chat" / "by phone") that the GT actually scores; the resolve_destination cross-origin refusal was irrelevant since same-destination is precisely the failure here.
classified.recommendation: Revise rubric link-purpose-v0 so that distinctRawHrefs=1 is NOT treated as a pass shortcut: when same-named, same-destination links sit in a context that promises distinct purposes (e.g. "via chat" vs "by phone"), require the model to flag a 2.4.4 barrier for misleading link purpose-in-context.

classified.rule: fd3a94  Links with identical accessible names and same context serve equivalent purpose
classified.realBarrier: fd3a94 tests whether two links sharing accessible name "Contact us" serve EQUIVALENT PURPOSE, not whether URLs differ. Both destinations (about/contact.html, careers/contact.html) share identical title, h1 "Contact us", and main content "Phone: (541) 754-3010"; only breadcrumb/submenu nav differs, so no 2.4.4 barrier exists and GT=passed is correct.

classified.rule: fd3a94
classified.realBarrier: fd3a94/2.4.4 fails when two links share an accessible name + context but resolve to DIFFERENT resources. This is the W3C canonical "Failed Example 3" (testcases.json: testcaseTitle "Failed Example 3", expected "failed"): hrefs are contact-us.html?page=1 (chat icon) and contact-us.html?page=2 (phone icon) — different destinations disambiguated only visually by CSS icons. The real barrier is two same-named "Contact Us" links going to distinct pages, so the identical-names-different-purpose failure mode genuinely applies.

This corrupted the deterministic sameNameLinks signal (llm-adjudicator.js:334-338) to distinctRawHrefs=1, on which the model explicitly relied: "distinctRawHrefs=1, meaning both same-named peers point to the same destination, ruling out the identical-names-different-purpose failure mode." With query strings intact distinctRawHrefs would be 2 and the failure triggers deterministically.
classified.recommendation: Fix the fixture-capture/mirroring step so it preserves href query strings (e.g. ?page=1/?page=2) instead of normalizing them away, so distinctRawHrefs reflects the true 2 distinct destinations for fd3a94 Failed Example 3.

classified.rule: fd3a94
classified.realBarrier: fd3a94 tests whether links sharing one accessible name in the same context serve an equivalent purpose. In this fixture two "Contact Us" links sit (via flex layout) directly under a "Chat" icon and a "Phone" icon respectively, so the surrounding context signals two DIFFERENT intended purposes (chat-contact vs phone-contact) that the identical name "Contact Us" fails to distinguish — W3C scores this exact file expected=failed. The barrier is the indistinguishable-name-against-distinct-visual-context, NOT a differing href (both hrefs are byte-identical contact-us.html), so destination resolution can never surface it.

The Chat/Phone surrounding-region context (declared in the rubric's visionEvidence) that drives the GT failure was never weighed because the href heuristic short-circuited it.
classified.recommendation: Revise link-purpose-v0.md so the "same destination ⇒ not a failure" carve-out is conditional: when surrounding-region shows distinct adjacent labels/icons (e.g. Chat vs Phone) that imply the identically-named links should serve DIFFERENT purposes, flag a 2.4.4 barrier even when distinctRawHrefs=1 / destinations are identical.

classified.rule: fd3a94

The fixture has two such links pointing to different LOCAL relative paths (.../b20e66/index.html vs .../b20e66/redirect1.html); the "redirect1" peer redirects to a different destination, so the identical names mislead — that is the real barrier and GT=failed.

The model reasoned correctly; the CDP resolver failed to follow same-origin local paths.
classified.recommendation: Fix resolve_destination so it follows same-origin/relative local test-asset paths (../_assets/...) instead of refusing them as cross-origin, so it can actually fetch and compare the two destinations' final URL/redirect targets and surface that index.html vs redirect1.html resolve to different content.

classified.rule: fd3a94  Links with identical accessible names and same context serve equivalent purpose
classified.realBarrier: ACT fd3a94 tests whether links sharing an identical accessible name + same context resolve to equivalent resources. This is W3C Failed Example 4: the two "Contact Us" links must differ by query string (`?page=60e950cff70bf1ec60a702086748ab4dec361514` vs `?page=c1d4e0f067462f4b28716f028d9213a25eb82f28`) — going to DIFFERENT resources, disambiguated only visually by the chat/phone images above. The real barrier is the differing destinations, which is the entire signal needed to score this failed.

Honest abstention rather than a flag, so GT=failed was missed (FN/recall).

The model's PARTIAL was the honest, correct response to the corrupted evidence ("if I can't confirm the destinations differ, I should return PARTIAL").

The THINK line — "this is a generic, non-descriptive name that doesn't convey the purpose of the control... a clear adequacy failure" — shows the model judged name descriptiveness, never the rule's actual focusable-content question, so a passing fixture was flagged FP.

classified.rule: fd3a94 Links with identical accessible names and same context serve equivalent purpose

It treated the aria-hidden link as a real same-named peer because the deterministic sameNameLinks signal handed it `distinctRawHrefs=2` and instructed it to call resolve_destination.

classified.realBarrier: ACT fd3a94 only applies to a SET of same-named links that ALSO share "the same programmatically determined link context" (rule Applicability line 35). The fixture is ACT's own Inapplicable Example 6 verbatim: two "Read more" links sit in SEPARATE sibling <div> blocks ("...about the W3C WAI" vs "...about the W3C internationalization"), so they are in DIFFERENT contexts and the rule never applies — GT=inapplicable, no barrier exists.

The model resolved destinations, saw finalUrlEqual=false, and flagged the identical-name/different-destination mode.

The model even saw the differing context ("Read more about the W3C WAI") but dismissed it (THINK: "the additional context doesn't disambiguate the link purpose"), a secondary misread downstream of the missing gate.

The real barrier is that the discriminating signal (the differing settled URLs page=1 vs page=2) never reached the model.

The model inferred wrongly: "Both links navigate and produce the same 'ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND' page... this indicates that both links point to the same destination" — when in fact both target files are merely missing on disk while the URLs (?page=1 vs ?page=2) differ.
classified.recommendation: Make resolve_destination extract and fingerprint onclick="location='...'" (and similar JS-navigation) targets — or have observe_state_after_activation return the post-navigation location.href — so the model can compare the differing ?page=1 vs ?page=2 URLs instead of being misled by identical ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND error-page content.

The fixture has two SVG-embedded <a> links both with aria-label="Contact Us" and the SAME href (contact-us.html), but the probe crop (out-svg-probe/fd3a94.png) shows two visually-distinct icons — a chat/speech bubble and a phone handset — i.e. two different contact methods presented under one undifferentiated name; ACT GT scores this failed. ## Cross-origin tool note

`resolve_destination` cross-origin refusal touches **exactly 3 cases**, all on the offline ACT corpus:

| Case | SC | Direction | Nature | Fixable offline? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `1379913f0770` | 2.4.4 (fd3a94) | FN | Resolver refused a **relative same-origin** local path (`../_assets/`) as cross-origin. | **Yes** — this is a resolver bug: `file://` same-origin local paths should resolve. Pure tool fix, no network. |
| `8e6c190e0d2b` | 2.4.4 (fd3a94 / 5effbb) | FP | Resolver refused to byte-compare two `file://` page bodies; returned only `finalUrlEqual:false` for equivalent-purpose pages. | **Yes but instrument-level** — teach the CDP tool to fetch and byte/DOM-compare local `file://` bodies. No network needed (corpus is mirrored locally), so it is achievable offline, just a larger tool upgrade than a prompt change. |
| `0b01e772dff4` | 2.4.4 (fd3a94) | FN | Not a resolver refusal per se — the **query string was stripped at capture**, so both hrefs resolve identically. | **No** — re-capture only. |

Quantified: **2 of the 31 FNs** are 2.4.4 cross-origin/resolver-adjacent (`1379913f0770` resolver refusal, `0b01e772dff4` capture artifact), and **1 of the 43 FPs** (`8e6c190e0d2b`). Of these, **2 are fixable entirely within the offline corpus** by relaxing/upgrading `resolve_destination` to handle same-origin `file://` paths and local body comparison; **1 (`0b01e772dff4`) is not** — it requires re-capturing the fixture because the discriminating signal no longer exists in the saved bytes. None require live network access, so the offline ACT corpus is not itself the blocker — the same-origin resolver policy is.
